description: RIDGE, the NEW astronaut health monitoring software is not trying to replace medical expertise in space. It is designed to make sure that expertise has the right information, at the right time.
summary:
Ridge is an astronaut-centred health monitoring and medical decision-support platform designed to support crew wellbeing and mission safety during long-duration spaceflight. Addressing five human-space hazards- space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity and hostile or closed environments Ridge  brings physical, psychological, cognitive and environmental health information into one integrated system.

It supports four categories of users, where Astronaut are the primary users, Flight Surgeons are the secondary users, Mission Control Unit are supporting users and Bio medical researchers are indirect users.
 
Beyond displaying individual readings, Ridge is designed to compare observations with personal baselines, visualise longitudinal trends and identify potentially important combinations of indicators. Context-aware alerts explain what has changed, why it may matter and what action should be considered. Its five-level Care Guidance framework: Green, Yellow and Red which supports graduated responses, from routine monitoring to emergency escalation, while preserving the authority of medical personnel.

It does not only for deep space operation but also isolated challenging environments in earth such as long duration analog missions, Antlantrica isolated research areas, in marine environments for sailors too when they have required medical models to take daily and weekly reading of their health indicators.
details:
The platform is designed to collect and organise physiological, psychological, cognitive and environmental health information through manual data entry, research datasets and, where supported, connected monitoring devices. It accommodates important clinical indicators, including heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature, blood glucose, oxygen saturation, symptoms, sleep patterns, hydration, nutrition, physical activity and medication records. It also considers behavioural-health indicators, cognitive performance, immune-system changes and environmental exposure information. Individual baseline comparisons, longitudinal trend analysis and cross-system indicator correlations help identify potentially significant changes that may require further attention. Its five-level Care Guidance framework – Green, Yellow and Red – provides structured, context-aware guidance ranging from routine self-monitoring to urgent escalation and emergency response, in accordance with authorised medical procedures.

An important scientific component of RIDGE is its integration with NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSDR). The development team implemented a dedicated NASA OSDR ingestion API endpoint that retrieves, unlocks and extracts compressed research-study archives. It then parses ISA-Tab metadata, including investigation, sample (s_.txt) and assay (a_.txt) files, making relevant research information accessible for further analysis. This integration provides a foundation for incorporating real spaceflight research into the platform, particularly studies concerning microgravity-associated immune dysregulation, latent viral reactivation and changes in spacecraft microbial populations. Such research data can support the exploration of baseline risk modelling, immune-system monitoring, microbial surveillance and potential environmental health risks.

RIDGE further integrates multiple external data sources to strengthen real-time spaceflight monitoring. The Lightstreamer API provides ISS environmental telemetry, including temperature, oxygen (O₂), carbon dioxide (CO₂) and nitrogen (N₂) levels. The WhereTheISS.at API provides the International Space Station's geographical position, while NASA's OSDR RadLab API provides radiation measurements, including absorbed dose rate and dose equivalent rate. Together, these integrations support environmental awareness, radiation surveillance and a more comprehensive understanding of conditions aboard the space station. The RIDGE interface has been adapted to bring these different data streams together through dedicated monitoring, visualisation and risk-assessment modules.

The primary benefit of RIDGE is its ability to bring together different sources of health and environmental information within one structured digital environment. Rather than treating each measurement independently, it considers relationships between physiological, psychological, cognitive and environmental indicators. This approach supports health awareness, longitudinal monitoring, improved medical documentation and more informed communication between astronauts and authorised medical teams. Its intended impact is to strengthen the capacity for health monitoring and medical decision support when immediate access to Earth-based healthcare is limited, contributing to safer and more sustainable human exploration missions.

RIDGE also incorporates a future development pathway involving an Internet of Things (IoT)-based plant-monitoring and automated irrigation system. The application interface has already been adapted to accommodate this planned integration, allowing astronauts to monitor plant-growing conditions and remotely control the watering mechanism once the hardware is implemented. Through future integration of environmental sensors, remote-control functionality and automated irrigation, the system aims to support plant maintenance, efficient resource use and controlled-environment food-production experiments in space. This feature extends the project's scope beyond individual health monitoring towards the wider environmental and sustainability requirements of long-duration missions.

An important aspect of RIDGE's development is its visual identity and user-interface design. The platform adopts a carefully selected Oat Ivory and Ink Blue colour palette, establishing a balance between a calm, approachable healthcare experience and the precision associated with aerospace technology. Oat Ivory provides a soft, neutral visual foundation that reduces visual harshness, while Ink Blue introduces contrast, structure and a sense of reliability across navigation elements, dashboards and information panels. The colour system is complemented by clear information hierarchies, structured data visualisations and distinguishable alert states to help astronauts interpret complex health and environmental information efficiently. This design approach aims to improve readability, consistency and usability in demanding operational environments.

The project's development is informed by aerospace medicine, biomedical science, human physiology, clinical monitoring principles, spaceflight research and digital health technologies. Its technical approach includes API-based research-data ingestion, structured metadata extraction, health-information visualisation, monitoring workflows and contextual alert logic. Relevant hardware considerations include portable clinical monitoring equipment, wearable sensors, environmental monitoring devices and the proposed IoT plant-monitoring unit. The exact programming languages, software frameworks and hardware components should be identified according to the technologies implemented by the development team.

Throughout development, the team considered physiological variation in microgravity, immune and microbial health risks, measurement reliability, data quality, individual health baselines, usability, accessibility, privacy, communication delays, limited medical resources and the importance of human clinical oversight. RIDGE is designed as a health-monitoring and medical decision-support platform rather than an autonomous diagnostic system. It does not replace qualified flight surgeons, independently prescribe treatment or authorise mission activities. Ultimately, RIDGE aims to transform scientific evidence and health observations into accessible, organised and actionable information, supporting astronaut wellbeing, informed medical decisions and the long-term sustainability of human space exploration.
